teaser: In 1782 Londoners lined up to be frightened by a painting. It still works.
review_notes:
Horace Walpole's one-word note 'shocking' in his copy of the 1782 Royal Academy catalogue: commonly cited.
Fuseli sold the painting for 20 guineas while the publisher of the 1783 engraving (by Thomas Burke) reportedly made over 500 pounds: commonly cited figures, check.
Unfinished portrait of a young woman on the back of the canvas, often thought to be Anna Landolt: the identification is a hypothesis.
A print of The Nightmare hanging in Freud's Vienna apartment is reported by Ernest Jones; often repeated.
The contents of the vial on the table are unknown; the lesson says so.
Second, upright version dated 1790-91 in the Goethe House museum, Frankfurt.
Detroit Institute of Arts acquired the painting in the 1950s.

lesson.text: London, spring 1782. At the Royal Academy's yearly exhibition, visitors push toward one canvas and then stand in front of it, not sure they should be looking. The writer Horace Walpole summed it up with one word in the margin of his catalogue: “shocking.” Within months the whole city knew the picture.

What unsettled them was partly what the painting was not. It illustrated no Bible story, no Greek myth, no scene from Shakespeare. Viewers of the time expected a serious picture to have a source they could name. This one seemed to come from nowhere except the inside of a sleeping head.

The painter was a 41-year-old Swiss immigrant, born Johann Heinrich Füssli in Zurich and trained as a Protestant minister. He had left his city after publicly accusing a corrupt official, drifted to London, and then spent eight years in Rome staring at Michelangelo's ceiling. He came back as Henry Fuseli, with a taste for huge muscles and extreme emotions.

lesson.title: Three in a bedroom
lesson.text: The room is almost black. Three figures come out of it, one at a time.

spots.title: The sleeper
spots.text: Her head hangs off the end of the bed, eyes shut, cheeks flushed, hair spilling down. Is she asleep, fainting, or dead? Fuseli leaves all three open.

spots.title: The thing on her
spots.text: A squat creature crouches on her body, chin on its fist like someone waiting. It is not looking at her. Its eyes are turned out of the picture, toward you.

spots.title: The horse
spots.text: A horse's head pushes through the curtain, mouth open, eyes like two white bulbs with no pupils. It glows as if lit from inside.

lesson.text: The creature has a name in old folklore: an incubus, a demon believed to sit on sleepers, especially women, and press the breath out of them. Today doctors would recognize the experience as sleep paralysis: you wake, cannot move, feel a weight on your chest and sense a presence in the room.

The “mare” in “nightmare” has nothing to do with horses. It comes from an old word for exactly this kind of spirit, one that rides on a sleeper's chest. Fuseli's horse is a visual pun on a word that only sounds like the animal.

So the picture shows two things at once: the woman as someone standing in the room would see her, and the dream as she feels it. That double view was the real novelty. How does Fuseli make you feel the weight?
The whole composition is designed around pressure.

lines.label: A bent bow
lines.text: From her pointed foot to her fingertips on the floor, the body makes one long arc, stretched far beyond what a real spine allows. She looks draped over the bed like cloth.

lines.label: The weight
lines.text: The demon sits at the highest point of that arc, straight above her belly. A compact dark block pressing down on a long pale curve: you read heaviness before you read anything else.

lines.label: Three heads
lines.text: Horse, demon and woman form a triangle. Two of its corners are awake and staring. The third, the lowest, cannot open her eyes.

lesson.text: Notice also where the light falls. Her white nightdress is the brightest thing in the room, yet there is no candle, no window, no moon. The glow has no source. Fuseli borrowed the trick from the theater, where a spotlit actor stands out against a dark stage, and London loved its theater.

Fuseli sold the painting for 20 guineas, a modest sum. The engraved copy published the next year, a print that could be run off by the hundreds, reportedly earned its publisher more than 500 pounds. The image made a fortune, mostly for someone else.

Those prints carried the scene across Europe, and cartoonists pounced. For decades, whenever a politician needed mocking, he was drawn sprawled on a bed with some goblin of a rival or a tax squatting on his chest. A painting had become what we would now call a meme.

Was it personal? A few years before, in Zurich, Fuseli had fallen violently in love with a young woman named Anna Landolt. Her father refused him and she married someone else. Some historians read the painting as jealous fantasy. He never explained it, and the room itself gives few clues. There is one corner worth checking.
The sleeper kept a few things within reach of her bed. Where are they?

spots.title: The bedside table
spots.text: A small round table with a lidded jar and a glass vial. Nobody knows what Fuseli meant the vial to hold. A medicine, a sleeping draft? It is the one hint of an ordinary cause.

lesson.text: That vial matters because it lets you choose. Either a demon is real and sitting in a London bedroom, or a woman has taken something and is dreaming badly. Fuseli paints both explanations with the same care and endorses neither.

The back of the canvas holds a surprise: an unfinished portrait of a young woman. It has often been suggested that she is Anna Landolt, which would put the lost love literally behind the nightmare. There is no proof.

The public wanted more, so Fuseli painted the subject again, including an upright version around 1790 in which the horse and the demon trade places. He became a professor at the Academy and a famous eccentric. None of his later pictures escaped the shadow of this one.
The Nightmare is among the first famous European paintings whose subject is a state of mind. It shows a fear from the inside, with no story to excuse it.

Its afterlife runs through horror itself. Mary Shelley, whose mother had known Fuseli well, laid a murdered bride across a bed in “Frankenstein” in a pose readers have long compared to this one. Sigmund Freud is said to have kept a print of it in his Vienna rooms. And the creature is still looking at you. What does it want you to do?

quiz.question: Why did the painting disturb visitors in 1782 beyond its subject?
options: It was painted on an enormous scale
It illustrated no known story from the Bible, myth or literature
It showed a real London crime
quiz.explanation: Viewers expected a serious picture to have a source they could name, and this one had none.

quiz.question: What is an incubus?
options: A demon believed to sit on sleepers and press on their chest
quiz.explanation: Folklore blamed this demon for the feeling of weight and suffocation in the night.

quiz.question: Where is the creature on the woman's body looking?
options: Out of the picture, at the viewer
quiz.explanation: Its eyes are turned toward you, not toward her.

quiz.question: What does the “mare” in “nightmare” originally mean?
options: A spirit that rides on a sleeper's chest
quiz.explanation: The word comes from an old name for a suffocating spirit, so the horse is a pun.

quiz.question: How did the image spread across Europe?
options: It was copied onto theater curtains
quiz.explanation: A print published the year after the exhibition sold widely and inspired many caricatures.

facts.text: Fuseli was born in Switzerland and first trained as a minister.
facts.explanation: He was born in Zurich, trained for the church, and only later became a painter in London.

facts.text: A candle on the bedside table lights the sleeping woman.
facts.explanation: There is no visible light source; the table holds only a jar and a vial.

facts.text: Fuseli painted the subject only once.
facts.explanation: Demand was so strong that he made further versions, including an upright one around 1790.
